documents.unit: Office of the Dean of the College / Scholarly Integrity
documents.title: Disclosing Generative AI Use (students)
documents.summary: Dean of the College scholarly-integrity page for students. It quotes Rights, Rules, Responsibilities 2.4: students must learn each course's AI rule, disclose permitted AI use rather than cite it, and failing to disclose is an integrity violation. It supplies a disclosure template and says courses range from no AI to open experimentation.
documents.stance_why: The page says "instructors may make generative AI off limits entirely. In others, limited use may be permitted," and the "first responsibility is always to determine whether, how, and to what extent a given course allows" AI. The university sets no AI stance of its own beyond the disclosure rule, so the decision is delegated to courses.

units.why: The page opens with a principle: "exciting—and it demands prudence." It sets a general tone for how students should approach AI, so it is a framing principle (general, informs), closest to an institution-level framework statement (P56).
units.anchor: Generative artificial intelligence technology is exciting—and it demands prudence.
units.frag_start: Generative artificial intelligence technology is
units.fit_note: Only a one-line framing; no scope or principles are spelled out.

units.why: Students "will want to exercise particular care in making sure you know when and how to use them", which tells students to learn the rules before using AI. This is closest to P10 (check before using), chosen over P04 because the actor is the student, not the instructor.
units.anchor: exercise particular care in making sure you know when and how to use them
units.frag_start: As generative AI technologies continue
units.fit_note: Frames a duty to know the rules, not specifically to ask the instructor when unsure.

units.why: "you will encounter a wide range of policies about generative AI depending on the learning goals for the course overall or for a particular assignment" says rules vary by course and assignment, so the instructor or assignment decides (P04).
units.anchor: you will encounter a wide range of policies about generative AI
units.frag_start: In your classes, you will

units.why: The passage lists three kinds of course policy: "off limits entirely", "limited use may be permitted", and courses inviting "experiment broadly". These are named categories of AI use, so P05; it is descriptive, hence informs and neutral.
units.anchor: instructors may make generative AI off limits entirely. In others, limited use may be permitted.
units.frag_start: In some cases, instructors may
units.frag_end: experiment broadly with these new tools.

units.why: "Your first responsibility is always to determine whether, how, and to what extent a given course allows you to use generative AI" makes finding out the course rule the student's duty. Nearest is P10; it is stated as a standing duty, not only when unsure.
units.anchor: to determine whether, how, and to what extent a given course allows you
units.frag_start: Your first responsibility
units.fit_note: Duty to determine the course rule itself; does not say to ask the instructor.

units.why: "When generative AI is permitted, your second responsibility is to always explicitly disclose your use of it" is a direct disclosure requirement on students (P24).
units.anchor: is to always explicitly disclose your use of it
units.frag_start: When generative AI is permitted,

units.why: The quoted RRR rule says "Students are responsible for familiarizing themselves with and adhering to course and departmental policies regarding the use of generative AI." This binds students to know and follow local rules, closest to P10; P04 does not fit because it is about the student duty.
units.anchor: Students are responsible for familiarizing themselves with and adhering to course and departmental policies
units.frag_start: Students are responsible for familiarizing
units.fit_note: Adds an adherence duty on top of learning the rule.

units.why: The RRR lists "representing output generated by or derived from generative AI as their own" as violations, so students must not submit AI output as their own work (P19).
units.anchor: representing output generated by or derived from generative AI as their own
units.frag_start: Inappropriate uses of the results
units.policy: Students may not directly copy generative AI output or represent output generated by or derived from generative AI as their own on any work submitted for an academic requirement.

units.why: "exceeding the parameters specified by the instructor" is named as a violation, so staying within the instructor's AI limits is required. It fits P04 (instructor sets the rule) only partly because it is also a misconduct definition.
units.anchor: exceeding the parameters specified by the instructor
units.frag_start: Inappropriate uses of the results
units.fit_note: Also defines exceeding instructor limits as an academic-integrity violation.

units.why: "failing to disclose its use, would constitute violations of academic integrity" makes nondisclosure itself the violation, which is the nondisclosure-as-violation half of P28.
units.anchor: failing to disclose its use, would constitute violations of academic integrity
units.frag_start: Inappropriate uses of the results

units.why: The RRR sentence says inappropriate uses "would constitute violations of academic integrity", classifying improper AI use as academic misconduct handled by integrity processes (P36).
units.anchor: would constitute violations of academic integrity
units.frag_start: Inappropriate uses of the results

units.why: "generative artificial intelligence (AI) is not a source, since its output" explains the reasoning behind disclosing rather than citing; it is a definition-like principle. Closest is P24 (disclosure) since the point is how AI is acknowledged.
units.anchor: generative artificial intelligence (AI) is not a source, since its output
units.frag_start: generative artificial intelligence (AI) is not a source
units.fit_note: States that AI is not a source, so disclosure replaces citation.

units.why: "students must disclose its use rather than cite or acknowledge the use" is a direct duty to disclose, with a specific form (disclosure, not citation). P24 covers disclosure; P25 (cite tool and prompt) does not fit because citation is rejected.
units.anchor: students must disclose its use rather than cite or acknowledge the use
units.frag_start: If generative AI is permitted by the
units.fit_note: Disclosure is required instead of citing or acknowledging.

units.why: "If generative AI is permitted by the instructor (for brainstorming, outlining, etc.)" gives example permitted uses, brainstorming and outlining, conditional on instructor permission (P15).
units.anchor: permitted by the instructor (for brainstorming, outlining, etc.)
units.frag_start: If generative AI is permitted by the
units.fit_note: Also covers outlining and makes permission depend on the instructor.

units.why: "students must not pass off any output by generative AI as their own" is a ban on submitting AI output as own work (P19).
units.anchor: students must not pass off any output by generative AI as their own
units.frag_start: All the tenets of scholarly integrity apply

units.why: "a failure of disclosure, even in a course where generative AI is permitted" makes nondisclosure the violation even where AI is allowed (P28).
units.anchor: a failure of disclosure, even in a course where generative AI is permitted
units.frag_start: All the tenets of scholarly integrity apply

units.why: "Check with your instructor about the disclosure template or use the template below" tells students to follow the instructor's disclosure form or the supplied one, a disclosure-with-submission rule (P24).
units.anchor: Check with your instructor about the disclosure template or use the template below.
units.frag_start: Check with your instructor about the disclosure

units.why: The template asks the student to state "which AI tool" and the "purpose" (brainstorming, outlining, revising, etc.). This is specified disclosure content, closest to P25 although prompt and output are not requested.
units.anchor: Specifically, I used
units.frag_start: This document was created with assistance
units.policy: The disclosure template has the student state which AI tool was used and for what purpose, such as brainstorming, outlining, generating content for sections of text, revising or proofreading text, or formatting citations.
units.fit_note: Tool and purpose only; no prompt or output required.

units.why: The template statement says "I have reviewed and edited this work and have retained records of my generative AI use", so the student attests to review and record keeping. Nearest is P26, but records are kept rather than submitted.
units.anchor: have retained records of my generative AI use
units.frag_start: This document was created with assistance
units.fit_note: Students attest to retaining records and to having reviewed and edited the work; records are not required to be submitted.

units.why: "different fields have different expectations for how to properly disclose" and MLA expects "a URL for accessing your conversation" shows disclosure and citation details can vary by discipline, and cites conversation links. P25 covers specific details of the citation.
units.anchor: the Modern Language Association expects you to provide much of the typical bibliographic information
units.frag_start: Be aware that different fields have
units.fit_note: Notes discipline-specific expectations and gives MLA as an example rather than requiring it.

units.why: "your practice with varied expectations across the University is itself good preparation for the varied norms you will encounter in the professional world" ties varied rules to professional readiness (P44), here as a reason rather than a skill to teach.
units.anchor: good preparation for the varied norms you will encounter in the professional world
units.frag_start: Keep in mind that your practice
units.fit_note: Frames adjusting to varied AI rules as career preparation, not teaching AI use.

units.why: "Some industries may have very strict use policies to assure client privacy, uphold license agreements, and protect data" explains that professional AI rules protect data and licences; it informs about norms. P44 is the nearest because the passage is about professional expectations.
units.anchor: very strict use policies to assure client privacy, uphold license agreements, and protect data
units.frag_start: Some industries may have very strict
units.fit_note: Mentions privacy and licence protections in industry, not a student data rule.

units.why: "employees understand the expectations of their field and exercise vigilance to ensure that generative AI use is within the guidelines" sets the professional expectation that people follow field rules, an analogy students are meant to learn from (P44).
units.anchor: exercise vigilance to ensure that generative AI use is within the guidelines
units.frag_start: But what unites all professional endeavors
units.fit_note: States the vigilance expectation for employees, used as analogy for students.

documents.unit: McGraw Center for Teaching and Learning
documents.title: Generative AI (McGraw Center)
documents.summary: Teaching-center landing page of faculty guidance on AI, with links to pages on setting a policy, assignment design, ethical risks, and detection. It states that faculty set AI policies for their courses and recommends against AI detectors. Most detail sits on linked subpages not captured here.
documents.stance_why: "Faculty are empowered to set AI policies for their courses" and the page offers "sample language you can use or adapt," so it sets no stance of its own and leaves the decision to instructors.

units.why: The page defines generative AI as creating "text, code, images, music" and contrasts it with predictive AI; defining terms sets what the guidance covers (P61).
units.anchor: Generative AI creates human-like output
units.frag_start: AI is not one thing but

units.why: "AI agents can act on your behalf" and "generates a sequence of steps to achieve and then executes on them" defines agentic AI, extending the guidance scope to autonomous tools (P61).
units.anchor: AI agents can act on your behalf
units.frag_start: Agentic AI is built on the same

units.why: The page asks "What risks does AI pose for student learning and development?" and "How does AI prompt us to reimagine our assignments?", setting out purpose and guiding questions, so a framework-like preamble (P56).
units.anchor: What risks does AI pose for student learning and development?
units.frag_start: As a set of technologies, AI asks us
units.fit_note: Poses guiding questions rather than stating principles.

units.why: "advise you to review the University's policies on AI" tells instructors to consult the RRR rules, so faculty policies must fit university rules (P77).

units.why: "We recognize that AI will continue to develop" and the page "will regularly update these pages" show the guidance is provisional (P54).

units.why: "Faculty are empowered to set AI policies for their courses" puts the decision with each instructor (P04).

documents.title: Disclosing the Use of AI (Library research guide)
documents.summary: Library research-guide page on disclosing AI use. It repeats the RRR rule that students must confirm instructor permission and disclose AI use, then mostly describes publisher and journal AI policies for researchers, and points to citation styles.
documents.stance_why: It says students "must confirm AI is permitted by an instructor and disclose the use of AI in any academic work," so permission is decided by instructors, and the rest summarizes publisher rules. It sets no stance of its own, so delegates.

units.why: "students must confirm AI is permitted by an instructor" requires checking that the instructor allows AI before use (P10).
units.anchor: must confirm AI is permitted by an instructor
units.frag_start: According to Princeton University's
units.fit_note: Phrased as a must-confirm permission condition rather than asking when unsure.

units.why: "disclose the use of AI in any academic work" is a blanket disclosure duty for students (P24).
units.anchor: disclose the use of AI in any academic work
units.frag_start: According to Princeton University's

units.why: "Princeton's AI disclosure policy aligns with broader conventions about AI and authorship in academic publishing" ties the student rule to publishing norms, within scholarship rules (P62).
units.anchor: aligns with broader conventions about AI and authorship in academic publishing
units.frag_start: Princeton's AI disclosure policy aligns

units.why: "AI tools do not meet the criteria for authorship for many publishers" and many "prohibit the use of AI-generated sources and images" describe publisher rules for research authors (P62).
units.anchor: AI tools do not meet the criteria for authorship for many publishers
units.frag_start: AI tools do not meet the criteria

units.why: "authors and reviewers should reach out to the publisher or editor to confirm their expectations" tells researchers to check venue rules when unstated (P62 defers to venue rules).
units.anchor: authors and reviewers should reach out to the publisher or editor
units.frag_start: If this information is not available

units.why: "AI-authored or co-authored sources cannot be cited. AI-generated images are also prohibited." reports the Science journals rule on AI in manuscripts (P62).
units.anchor: AI-authored or co-authored sources cannot be cited.
units.frag_start: Science states that AI does not meet

units.anchor: should note this in the cover letter and in the methods section or acknowledgments section
units.frag_start: Authors who use AI-assisted technologies

units.why: "Authors are accountable for the accuracy of the work and for ensuring that there is no plagiarism" with review "to guard against bias" is a venue accountability rule (P62), not a student course rule.
units.anchor: Authors are accountable for the accuracy of the work
units.frag_start: Authors are accountable for the accuracy
units.fit_note: Combines accountability, verification and bias checks in a publisher rule.

units.why: "While some AI tools are permissible for use without disclosure (e.g., grammar checkers)" reports an Elsevier exemption from disclosure for grammar checkers (P62).
units.anchor: some AI tools are permissible for use without disclosure (e.g., grammar checkers)

units.why: Elsevier "requires that the AI tools be disclosed in the manuscript" under a named declaration; it is a venue disclosure rule (P62).
units.anchor: requires that the AI tools be disclosed in the manuscript
units.frag_start: Elsevier's policy on the use of generative AI

units.why: "Authors should document their use of AI, including the name of the AI Tool used, the purpose of the use, and the extent of their oversight" lists details a disclosure must contain (P62 for research; also resembles P25).
units.anchor: the name of the AI Tool used, the purpose of the use, and the extent
units.frag_start: Authors should document their use of AI
units.fit_note: Details of an Elsevier declaration; tool, purpose and oversight rather than prompt.

units.why: "it is important to review publisher policies for changes for each project or review you submit" tells researchers that publisher rules change and must be rechecked (P62).
units.anchor: it is important to review publisher policies for changes
units.frag_start: Note that this is a rapidly developing field
units.fit_note: Also notes that policies change regularly.

units.why: "Tools and use taxonomies are being developed to help identify AI use and draft disclosure statements" presents disclosure-statement builders that students may use as a starting point (P24).
units.anchor: draft disclosure statements for a variety of use cases
units.frag_start: Tools and use taxonomies are being developed
units.fit_note: Optional tools to draft statements; they may not meet an instructor's or publisher's full requirements.

units.why: "Different citation styles take different approaches, so check with the citation style preferred by your field and the publisher" tells writers to follow the field's AI citation style (P25).
units.anchor: check with the citation style preferred by your field and the publisher
units.frag_start: Different citation styles take different approaches
units.fit_note: Defers citation details to the style guide; no details are specified here.

notes: Coder B. Princeton has no single university AI policy page; RRR 2.4 was not collected and is known only through quotes in the scholarly-integrity page. McGraw linked subpages (setting a policy, detection, etc.) were not collected, so only the landing page is coded.
